bottles.name: Aperol
desc: Light Italian aperitif with bitter orange and a touch of sweetness.
Fresh and easy to drink, perfect for Spritz or as a pre-dinner drink.
bottles.edge: Half the alcohol of Campari and much sweeter — orange and rhubarb where Campari is bitter orange peel. The Spritz default.

bottles.name: Campari
desc: Bold Italian aperitif, bitter with orange and herbal notes.
Stronger and drier than Aperol, perfect for Negroni, Spritz, or Americano.
bottles.edge: The anchor for the whole shelf: the most bitter of the mainstream aperitivi and the driest. If a bottle is described as “less bitter”, this is what it is less bitter than.

bottles.name: Pilla Select
desc: Italian aperitif with a more herbal and complex profile, featuring citrus notes and balanced bitterness.
Less sweet than Aperol, great for a Spritz with more character.
bottles.origin: Italy — Venice (Veneto). Brand is "Select", created by the Pilla family in 1920.
bottles.edge: The Venetian original behind the local Spritz: bitterer than Aperol, sweeter than Campari, with a distinct rhubarb and juniper note.

bottles.name: Rosso Antico Aperitivo
desc: Red Italian aperitif, smooth and aromatic, with bitter orange, herbs, spices and a touch of sweetness.
Softer and less aggressive than Campari
bottles.edge: Softer and more vanilla-sweet than Campari, low in bitterness. An easy red for a guest who finds Campari too harsh.

bottles.name: Aperitivo Capo
desc: Fresh and citrusy Italian aperitif, with orange, Mediterranean herbs and gentle bitterness.
Lighter and easier to drink than Campari
bottles.fact: Founded in 1915 by Giuseppe Caffo near Mount Etna, Sicily; the family distillery later moved to Calabria.
bottles.edge: Calabrian citrus-led: more orange and bergamot, far less bitter bark than Campari.

bottles.name: Aperitivo del Professore
desc: Artisanal Italian aperitif, citrusy and herbal, with bitter orange, soft spice and balanced bitterness.
More refined and less commercial than Aperol
bottles.fact: Created in 2013 by bartender Leonardo Leuci, named for 19th-century bartender Jerry “The Professor” Thomas.
bottles.edge: A craft red bitter: drier and more herbal-complex than Campari, with less sugar and more spice.
bottles.tier: Premium for the scale and recipe: small-batch bartender production with a broader botanical bill than industrial bitters.

bottles.name: Carpano Botanic Bitter
desc: Red Italian bitter, herbal and citrusy, with bitter orange, spice and an elegant bitterness.
Drier and more complex than Aperol, but less aggressive than some very intense bitters
bottles.fact: Invented in 1786 by Antonio Benedetto Carpano — the first modern vermouth, infused with 30+ herbs and spices in Turin.
bottles.edge: Carpano’s bitter — rounder and more aromatic than Campari, with visible vanilla and citrus from the house style.

bottles.name: Italicus Bergamotto
desc: Fresh and aromatic Italian aperitif with bergamot, citrus, and floral notes.
Light and elegant, perfect for delicate Spritz or refreshing cocktails.
bottles.origin: Italy — Bergamot from Calabria; produced in the Bologna area (Emilia-Romagna)
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: Not a bitter at all: a pale bergamot liqueur, floral and sweet-citric. The lightest bottle on this shelf and the one that goes with prosecco or tonic.
bottles.tier: Premium for the fruit: Calabrian bergamot and Sicilian cedro, both hand-pressed citrus with no industrial substitute.

bottles.name: Savoia
desc: Red Italian aperitif, elegant and aromatic, with bitter orange, spice, herbs, and a sweet-bitter touch.
It has a more wine-like and refined profile than a simple bitter
bottles.origin: Italy — created by Giuseppe Gallo (also creator of Italicus)
bottles.edge: A dark, cocoa-and-orange Italian bitter — sweeter and rounder than Campari, closer to a light amaro.

bottles.name: Starlino Aperitivo Orange
desc: Fresh and citrusy Italian aperitif, with orange, grapefruit, herbs and gentle bitterness.
Fruitier and easier to drink than Campari
bottles.edge: The sweetest orange aperitivo here: soft, low bitterness, made for Spritz with a guest who finds Aperol too sharp.

bottles.name: Starlino Aperitivo Rosso
desc: Red Italian aperitif, smooth and aromatic, with bitter orange, herbs, spices and a touch of sweetness.
Rounder and less aggressive than Campari
bottles.fact: Launched in 2020 by Malfy Gin founder Elwyn Gladstone, made at Piedmont's century-old Torino Distillati.
bottles.edge: A red bitter in the Campari mould but noticeably sweeter and softer, with more red fruit.

bottles.name: Zucca Rabarbaro
desc: Bold Italian aperitif with rhubarb, smoky notes, and deep bitterness.
Darker and more serious.
bottles.edge: Built on Chinese rhubarb root, not citrus: smoky, earthy and gently bitter — the odd one out on this shelf, and excellent with soda.

bottles.name: Bordiga Bitter Verde
desc: Herbal Italian aperitif with fresh green notes and a subtle anise touch.
Lighter and less aggressive than Campari
bottles.edge: Green, not red: alpine herbs and mint instead of bitter orange. The most unusual bitter here and the reason to build a green Negroni.
bottles.tier: Premium for the botanicals: mountain herbs from the Cuneo valleys, distilled on wood-fired alembics, with no artificial colouring.

bottles.name: Cocchi Americano
desc: Italian wine-based aperitif with citrus notes and gentle bitterness.
Fresh and elegant — similar to a white vermouth
serves: Vesper Martini (as the Kina Lillet swap)
On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: A quinine-based aperitivo wine, not a bitter liqueur: lower in alcohol, lighter, with a gentian bitterness and citrus lift. The classic stand-in for Kina Lillet.
bottles.tier: Premium for the base: Moscato d’Asti wine infused with cinchona bark, which is what gives it the delicate grape aroma under the bitterness.

bottles.name: Cocchi Americano Rossa
desc: Italian wine-based aperitif with red fruit, spice, and gentle bitterness.
Richer and fuller than the white
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Cocchi macerates its botanicals in small batches, extracting each ingredient separately before blending into the wine base.
bottles.edge: The red sibling: same quinine backbone but on a red wine base, so darker fruit and more spice than the white.
bottles.tier: Premium for the same Piedmont wine base, here on Brachetto-style red fruit.

bottles.name: Mancino Rinomato Aperitivo
desc: Italian aperitif with citrus and herbal notes and balanced bitterness.
More elegant and less sweet than Aperol — great for refined Spritz or softer Negronis.
bottles.edge: A wine-based aperitivo in the Cocchi Americano family: lighter than Campari, with gentian bitterness and a clean citrus finish.
bottles.tier: Premium for Mancino’s individually-infused botanical process.

bottles.name: Mancino Rinomato Scuro
desc: Darker, more intense Italian aperitif with spice and deeper bitterness.
Less fresh than the Aperitivo
bottles.fact: Mancino mills and infuses 40 botanicals for 30 days each on a 1930s mill, then rests six months.
bottles.edge: The darker Rinomato: more bitter root and cacao than the standard, still on a wine base rather than spirit.
bottles.tier: Premium for the same long-infusion process, here with a deeper bitter-root selection.

bottles.name: Martini Bitter
desc: Red Italian aperitif with bitter, citrus, and herbal notes.
Drier and sharper than Aperol, but a bit softer than Campari.
bottles.fact: Founded in 1863 in Pessione, Turin, by Alessandro Martini, winemaker Luigi Rossi and accountant Teofilo Sola.
bottles.edge: Martini’s answer to Campari: the same red-bitter role, slightly sweeter and less aggressive on the finish.

bottles.name: Martini Rosso
desc: Sweet Italian vermouth with herbal, vanilla, and soft caramel notes.
Easy to drink and very versatile
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Founded in 1863 in Pessione, Turin, by Alessandro Martini, winemaker Luigi Rossi and accountant Teofilo Sola.
bottles.edge: The anchor. Every other rosso is described as sweeter, drier or more bitter than this one. Caramel and light herbs, nothing sharp.

bottles.name: Martini Bianco
desc: White Italian vermouth, soft and aromatic, with vanilla, floral notes, and a herbal touch.
Sweeter and more delicate than dry vermouth
bottles.fact: Founded in 1863 in Pessione, Turin, by Alessandro Martini, winemaker Luigi Rossi and accountant Teofilo Sola.
bottles.edge: Sweeter and more vanilla-led than Martini Rosso, with no bitterness at all. The white a guest will like even if they say they hate vermouth.

bottles.name: Martini Extra Dry
desc: Dry Italian vermouth, light and fresh, with herbal notes, soft citrus, and a floral touch.
Less sweet than Martini Bianco
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Founded in 1863 in Pessione, Turin, by Alessandro Martini, winemaker Luigi Rossi and accountant Teofilo Sola.
bottles.edge: Half the sugar of Bianco and far more citric. Its job is to disappear behind the gin in a Dry Martini.

bottles.name: Martini Riserva Speciale Rubino
desc: Premium red Italian vermouth with more body than Martini Rosso, showing spice, herbs, and dark fruit notes.
Deeper and more elegant
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Founded in 1863 in Pessione, Turin, by Alessandro Martini, winemaker Luigi Rossi and accountant Teofilo Sola.
bottles.edge: Martini Rosso with the volume up: darker fruit, more spice, longer bitter finish.
bottles.tier: Premium for the wine and the botanicals: a Langhe DOC wine base instead of a neutral blend, plus Italian-grown red sandalwood and rare wormwood. You taste it as more depth of dark fruit and a drier, more savoury finish than the standard Rosso.

bottles.name: Martini Riserva Speciale Ambrato
desc: Premium white Italian vermouth, more aromatic and complex than Martini Bianco, with floral notes, soft honey, herbs, and a citrus touch.
Elegant and delicate
bottles.fact: Founded in 1863 in Pessione, Turin, by Alessandro Martini, winemaker Luigi Rossi and accountant Teofilo Sola.
bottles.edge: Where Bianco goes vanilla-sweet, Ambrato goes honey and chamomile — golden, aromatic, noticeably less sugary.
bottles.tier: Premium for the grape: a Moscato d’Asti-led base instead of neutral white wine, with Chinese rhubarb. That grape is why it smells of orchard fruit and honey where Bianco smells of vanilla.

bottles.name: Cinzano Rosso
desc: Red Italian vermouth, sweet and spiced, with herbal notes, dark fruit, and a touch of vanilla.
Similar to Martini Rosso, but slightly more spiced
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Turin's Cinzano family became Master Distillers on 6 January 1757 — the date the brand still carries in its name.
bottles.edge: Same role as Martini Rosso but spicier — more clove and dark fruit, a touch less caramel.

bottles.name: Cinzano Bianco
desc: White Italian vermouth, soft and aromatic, with vanilla, herbs, and a floral touch.
Sweet and easy to drink
bottles.fact: Turin's Cinzano family became Master Distillers on 6 January 1757 — the date the brand still carries in its name.
bottles.edge: Sweeter and rounder than Martini Bianco, with more floral lift. The easiest pour on the shelf with soda and a slice of lemon.

bottles.name: Cinzano Extra Dry
desc: Dry Italian vermouth, fresh and light, with herbal notes, soft citrus, and a floral touch.
Less sweet than Cinzano Bianco
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: The lightest, cleanest dry here — drier than Carpano Dry and with less herbal weight than Cocchi Extra Dry.

bottles.name: Cinzano 1757 Rosso
desc: Premium red Italian vermouth with more body and depth than classic Cinzano Rosso. It has spice, herbs, dark fruit, and a sweet-bitter touch.
Richer and more elegant
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: The founding year on the label. Richer and more bitter than standard Cinzano Rosso: cocoa and dark spice instead of simple sweetness.
bottles.tier: Premium for the process: longer maceration on a higher-quality wine base, aged briefly in oak. That is where the cocoa depth and the drier finish come from.

bottles.name: Cinzano 1757 Extra Dry
desc: Premium dry Italian vermouth, cleaner and more elegant than classic Cinzano Extra Dry. It has herbal, citrus, and floral notes, with a fresh, clean finish.
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: A dry with actual aroma — more floral and precise than the standard Extra Dry, still bone dry.
bottles.tier: Premium for the botanical selection and a finer wine base; the pay-off is aroma, not sweetness.

bottles.name: Carpano Classico
desc: Classic Italian red vermouth, sweet and herbal, with spice, red fruit, and a touch of vanilla.
It has more body than a basic red vermouth
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Invented in 1786 by Antonio Benedetto Carpano — the first modern vermouth, infused with 30+ herbs and spices in Turin.
bottles.edge: From the house that invented vermouth in 1786. More body and red fruit than Martini Rosso, less bitter than Punt e Mes.

bottles.name: Carpano Bianco
desc: White Italian vermouth, soft and aromatic, with vanilla, herbs, and a citrus touch.
More delicate and rounded than a dry vermouth
bottles.fact: Invented in 1786 by Antonio Benedetto Carpano — the first modern vermouth, infused with 30+ herbs and spices in Turin.
bottles.edge: Heavier and more vanilla-driven than Martini Bianco; closer to a dessert vermouth than to a dry.

bottles.name: Carpano Dry
desc: Dry Italian vermouth, fresh and clean, with herbal notes, soft citrus, and a drier finish.
Less sweet than Carpano Bianco
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: The house style stripped back: drier than Carpano Bianco but with more herbal grip than Martini Extra Dry.

bottles.name: Carpano Punt e Mes
desc: Italian red vermouth, sweet-bitter and full of character. It has herbal, spice, dark fruit notes, and a more noticeable bitterness than a classic rosso vermouth.
More intense than Carpano Classico
bottles.edge: Dialect for “point and a half”: one point of sweet, half a point of bitter. The only rosso here that is openly half-amaro — pour it when a Negroni needs more edge.

bottles.name: Carpano Antica Formula
desc: Premium Italian red vermouth, rich and elegant, with vanilla, spice, dried fruit, and herbal notes.
More luxurious and fuller than a classic rosso vermouth
bottles.fact: Invented in 1786 by Antonio Benedetto Carpano — the first modern vermouth, infused with 30+ herbs and spices in Turin.
bottles.edge: The heaviest, sweetest, most aromatic rosso on the shelf: vanilla, dried fig and saffron. One measure rebuilds a whole Manhattan.
bottles.tier: Premium for the botanical load and the recipe: the 1786 formula with real vanilla and a very high herb concentration on a rich wine base. Next to Martini Rosso it is thicker in the mouth, twice as aromatic and much longer on the finish — which is why it is a sipping vermouth, not a filler.

bottles.name: Cocchi Rosso di Torino
desc: Italian red vermouth, elegant and aromatic, with cacao, spice, herbs, and dark fruit notes.
Deeper and more refined than a basic rosso
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Cocchi macerates its botanicals in small batches, extracting each ingredient separately before blending into the wine base.
bottles.edge: More cocoa and citrus peel than Martini Rosso, and drier on the finish. The stirred-drink specialist’s rosso.
bottles.tier: Premium for the method: every botanical is macerated separately in Asti and blended afterwards, so each note stays distinct instead of blurring together.

bottles.name: Cocchi Dopo Teatro
desc: Dark and intense Italian red vermouth, with cacao, spices, herbs, and a more noticeable bitterness.
Deeper and more bitter than Cocchi Torino
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: “After theatre” — the darkest, most bitter Cocchi: more bitter than its own Rosso di Torino and built to be drunk late and neat.
bottles.tier: Premium for the base: a Moscato-fortified wine with a higher share of bitter botanicals and longer ageing than the house Rosso.

bottles.name: Cocchi Extra Dry
desc: Dry Italian vermouth, fresh and elegant, with herbs, soft citrus, and a light floral touch.
Cleaner and more refined than a basic dry vermouth
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Cocchi macerates its botanicals in small batches, extracting each ingredient separately before blending into the wine base.
bottles.edge: A dry vermouth with aroma: herbal and floral where Martini and Cinzano Extra Dry go clean and blank.

bottles.name: Cocchi Chinato
desc: Aromatic Italian vermouth with a sweet-bitter profile, showing spice, cacao, dark fruit, and elegant bitterness.
Deeper and more digestive than a classic rosso vermouth
bottles.fact: Cocchi macerates its botanicals in small batches, extracting each ingredient separately before blending into the wine base.
bottles.edge: Quinine bark rather than bitter orange — a drier, more medicinal bitterness than any rosso. Digestivo first, mixer second.

bottles.name: Cocchi Barolo Chinato
desc: Premium Italian vermouth-style aromatised wine made with Barolo, deep and elegant, with dark fruit, cacao, spice, herbs, and fine bitterness.
More wine-driven and digestive than a classic rosso vermouth
bottles.origin: Italy — Asti (Piedmont); made with Barolo wine
bottles.edge: The only bottle on the shelf built on Barolo. It drinks as wine first: Nebbiolo tannin, then quinine and cacao.
bottles.tier: Premium for the grape and the appellation: Nebbiolo from Barolo DOCG, the most expensive wine base in the category. That grape gives the tannic grip and dried-rose perfume no neutral-wine chinato can produce.

bottles.name: Oscar 697 Rosso
desc: Modern Italian red vermouth, aromatic, with herbs, spices, red fruit, and a sweet-bitter touch.
Fresher and easier to drink than some heavier red vermouths
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Created by Oreste Sconfi of Piedmont's La Canellese (est. 1957) with Milanese bartender Oscar Quagliarini.
bottles.edge: A bartender’s rosso — fresher and lighter than Carpano or Cocchi, less sweet than Martini Rosso. Made in Piedmont with Milan’s Oscar Quagliarini.

bottles.name: Oscar 697 Bianco
desc: White Italian vermouth, fresh and aromatic, with floral, citrus, and a herbal touch.
Lighter and less sweet than other classic white vermouths
bottles.fact: Created by Oreste Sconfi of Piedmont's La Canellese (est. 1957) with Milanese bartender Oscar Quagliarini.
bottles.edge: The least sweet bianco on the shelf: floral and citric, closer to a dry than to Martini Bianco.

bottles.name: Oscar 697 Extra Dry
desc: Dry Italian vermouth, fresh and modern, with herbal, citrus notes and a clean finish.
Drier and less sweet than Oscar 697 Bianco
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: A modern dry: crisp, short, no residual sweetness at all — the driest of the three Oscar bottles.

bottles.name: Chazalettes & Co Rosso Torino
desc: Red vermouth from Torino, aromatic and elegant, with herbs, spices, red fruit, orange and a light bitter touch.
More classic and refined than a basic rosso
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Founded in Turin in 1876; in 1907 Queen Margherita granted the house the Royal coat of arms.
bottles.edge: A revived 1876 Turin recipe carrying the Royal coat of arms granted by Queen Margherita in 1907. Drier and more herbal than Martini Rosso, with a bitter-orange finish.
bottles.tier: Premium for the recipe and the scale: an archive Turin formula bottled in small runs. It reads more austere and less sweet than industrial rossi.

bottles.name: Naturale Rosso
desc: Italian red vermouth with a fresher, more natural profile, showing herbs, soft spice, red fruit and a light bitter touch.
Less heavy than some classic red vermouths
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: The only non-Piedmont vermouth here, made by the COS estate in Sicily. Fresher, much less sweet, and the grape actually shows through.
bottles.tier: Premium for the wine: a natural, unfiltered Sicilian estate wine instead of an industrial blend, with low added sugar. Next to Martini Rosso it tastes drier, more citric and more like wine than syrup.

bottles.name: Bordiga Rosso
desc: Red Italian bitter with herbal, citrus notes and a clear but elegant bitterness.
More artisanal and less commercial than Campari
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Herbalist Pietro Bordiga founded the distillery in Cuneo in 1888; it still uses wood-fired copper alembics.
bottles.edge: Filed under vermouth but drinks like a red bitter: more herbal and citric than any other rosso here, with far less sugar.

bottles.name: Bordiga Excelsior
desc: Premium Italian red vermouth with full body, spice, herbs, dark fruit, and elegant bitterness.
Deeper and more intense than a classic rosso vermouth
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Herbalist Pietro Bordiga founded the distillery in Cuneo in 1888; it still uses wood-fired copper alembics.
bottles.edge: Full-bodied and bitter-edged — as rich as Antica Formula but drier and more alpine-herbal instead of vanilla-sweet.
bottles.tier: Premium for the house and the herbs: founded by an herbalist in Cuneo in 1888, still distilling on wood-fired copper alembics with mountain botanicals. That is what puts the resinous alpine note in it.

bottles.name: Vermouth del Professore Rosso
desc: Artisanal Italian red vermouth, aromatic, with spice, herbs, ripe fruit, and a bitter touch.
More complex and elegant than a classic rosso
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Created in 2013 by bartender Leonardo Leuci, named for 19th-century bartender Jerry “The Professor” Thomas.
bottles.edge: Riper fruit and a sharper bitter edge than Martini Rosso, with a rustic, slightly cloudy character. Named for Jerry “The Professor” Thomas.

bottles.name: Vermouth del Professore Superiore
desc: Premium Italian amber vermouth with spice, herbs, orange, and a touch of vanilla.
More complex and structured than a classic white vermouth
bottles.fact: Created in 2013 by bartender Leonardo Leuci, named for 19th-century bartender Jerry “The Professor” Thomas.
bottles.edge: The amber of the pair: orange peel, vanilla and real structure. Sweeter than Mancino Ambrato, more aromatic than Martini Ambrato.
bottles.tier: Premium for the production: small-batch artisanal blending by bartenders, with a wider botanical bill and a longer rest than the house Rosso. It is built to be sipped over ice on its own.

bottles.name: Starlino Vermouth Rosso
desc: Smooth and aromatic Italian red vermouth, with vanilla, spice, herbs, red fruit and a touch of orange.
Rounder and easier to drink than a very intense rosso vermouth
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Launched in 2020 by Malfy Gin founder Elwyn Gladstone, made at Piedmont's century-old Torino Distillati.
bottles.edge: The softest, most orange-led rosso on the shelf — sweeter and rounder than Martini Rosso, with almost no bitterness. Launched in 2020 by the founder of Malfy Gin.

bottles.name: Mancino Rosso
desc: Elegant and balanced Italian red vermouth, with spice, herbs, red fruit, and a touch of vanilla.
More refined and aromatic than a basic rosso
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.fact: Mancino mills and infuses 40 botanicals for 30 days each on a 1930s mill, then rests six months.
bottles.edge: Precision rather than power: cleaner and less sweet than Carpano, with the herbs arriving one at a time instead of all at once.
bottles.tier: Premium for the process: 40 botanicals milled on a 1930s mill and infused individually for 30 days, then six months’ rest before bottling. That long rest is why it tastes integrated and silky rather than sharp.

bottles.name: Mancino Bianco Ambrato
desc: Italian white/amber vermouth, aromatic and delicate, with floral notes, soft honey, herbs, and a citrus touch.
Drier and more elegant than many sweet white vermouths
bottles.fact: Mancino mills and infuses 40 botanicals for 30 days each on a 1930s mill, then rests six months.
bottles.edge: An amber that goes dry, not sweet: honey and chamomile with a clean finish. The opposite of Martini Bianco.
bottles.tier: Premium for the same 40-botanical, individually-infused process as the house Rosso — the reason it stays delicate where sweeter ambers turn heavy.

bottles.name: Mancino Secco
desc: Dry Italian vermouth, fresh and elegant, with herbal notes, soft citrus, and a clean finish.
Drier and more precise than Mancino Bianco Ambrato
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: The most precise dry here: tighter and more herbal than Martini Extra Dry, with nothing sweet to hide behind.

bottles.name: Mancino Chinato
desc: Intense and digestive Italian vermouth with spice, herbs, dark fruit, and elegant bitterness.
Deeper and more bitter than a classic rosso — great after dinner
bottles.edge: Quinine and dark fruit — deeper and more bitter than Mancino Rosso, and less wine-driven than Cocchi Barolo Chinato.

bottles.name: Mancino Kopi
desc: Italian red vermouth infused with coffee, with espresso, cacao, spice, and herbal notes.
Darker and more aromatic than a classic rosso
bottles.edge: The coffee one. A rosso infused with espresso and cacao — nothing else on the shelf tastes like it.

bottles.name: Vermouth Stellare Primo
desc: Modern and aromatic Italian red vermouth, with herbs, spices, red fruit and a citrus-bitter touch.
Elegant but easy to drink
serves: On the rocks with a twist
bottles.edge: Antica Torino’s modern rosso: light and citrus-bitter, less sweet than Martini Rosso. The first vermouth to hand a guest who says they don’t like vermouth.

bottles.name: Amaro Averna
desc: Dark Italian amaro, smooth and sweet-bitter, with orange, caramel, herbs, spices and liquorice notes.
Rounder and easier to drink than more aggressive amaros
bottles.edge: The easy middle of the shelf: sweeter than Montenegro, far less bitter than Fernet. Caramel, orange peel and liquorice.

bottles.name: Amaro Montenegro
desc: Smooth Italian amaro, floral and citrusy, with orange, herbs, soft spices and a sweet-bitter touch.
Lighter and easier to drink than Averna
bottles.fact: Created in 1885 by Stanislao Cobianchi as “Elisir Lungavita,” renamed in 1896 for Princess Elena of Montenegro.
bottles.edge: The most floral and orange-led amaro here — light bitterness, high aromatics. The one to give a guest who has never had amaro.

bottles.name: Amaro Lucano
desc: Balanced Italian amaro, herbal and sweet-bitter, with orange, herbs, spices and a touch of caramel.
It has more character than Montenegro, but feels lighter than Averna
bottles.edge: Drier and more herbal than Averna, with a bitter-root finish instead of caramel sweetness.

bottles.name: Amaro del Capo
desc: Italian amaro from Calabria, smooth and sweet-bitter, with herbs, orange, liquorice, mint and spice notes.
Fresher and easier to drink than darker amaros
bottles.edge: The sweetest amaro on the shelf: liquorice, mint and orange, served ice cold from the freezer.

bottles.name: Amaro del Capo Riserva 100 anni
desc: Premium version of Amaro del Capo, more intense, deeper and more elegant.
It keeps the herbal, citrus and spiced notes, but with more body and complexity
bottles.fact: Founded in 1915 by Giuseppe Caffo near Mount Etna, Sicily; the family distillery later moved to Calabria.
bottles.edge: Del Capo aged in oak: less sugary, more vanilla and spice, with real length instead of a sweet finish.
bottles.tier: Premium for the ageing: rested in Amarone barrels, which is where the vanilla, dried fruit and drier finish come from. Side by side with standard Capo it tastes rounder and considerably less sweet.

bottles.name: Amaro Nonino
desc: Elegant and balanced Italian amaro, with orange, herbs, spices, soft honey and a touch of caramel.
More delicate and refined than many dark amaros
bottles.fact: In 1992 the Nonino sisters swapped the family amaro's grappa base for aged grape distillate, creating Quintessentia.
bottles.edge: Grappa-based rather than neutral-spirit-based, so it is lighter and more aromatic than Averna, with a distinct grape spirit note.
bottles.tier: Premium for the base spirit: built on Nonino grappa aged in barriques, not neutral alcohol. That is why it smells of grape and oak instead of caramel.

bottles.name: Amaro Nonino Riserva
desc: More premium and aged version of Amaro Nonino, deeper, more elegant and fuller-bodied.
It keeps the orange, herbs, spices and soft honey notes, but adds more oak, warmth and complexity
bottles.edge: The Quintessentia taken further: longer barrel ageing gives more oak, dried apricot and a drier, longer finish than the standard Nonino.
bottles.tier: Premium for the extended cask ageing on an already grappa-based amaro — the most refined bottle on this shelf and a sipping pour.

bottles.name: Amaro Ramazzotti
desc: Classic Italian amaro, sweet-bitter and spiced, with orange, herbs, cinnamon, clove and soft caramel notes.
Warmer and more spiced than Montenegro
bottles.edge: Milanese and cola-like: sweeter and rounder than Lucano, with orange and star anise. A crowd-pleaser with tonic.

bottles.name: Amaro Tosolini
desc: Northern Italian amaro, herbal and elegant, with alpine herbs, citrus, soft spices and balanced bitterness.
Drier and more refined than very sweet amaros
bottles.fact: Bepi Tosolini's 1918 recipe blends 15 herbs, including lagoon-gathered sea wormwood, aged in a salted cellar.
bottles.edge: Friulian, grappa-influenced and drier than Averna, with mountain herbs rather than caramel.

bottles.name: Amaro Trentino
desc: Northern Italian amaro, herbal and fresh, with alpine herbs, citrus, soft spices and a clean bitterness.
Drier and more mountain-style than sweeter amaros
bottles.edge: Alpine style: mint, pine and gentian, lighter in body and less sweet than the southern amari.

bottles.name: Amaro Alpe
desc: Italian alpine-style amaro, herbal and fresh, with mountain herbs, mint, soft spices and a clean bitterness.
Drier and more refreshing than dark amaros like Averna
bottles.edge: Genepy-adjacent alpine herbs — greener and fresher than any southern amaro, low sugar.

bottles.name: Amaro Dilei
desc: Italian amaro by Bordiga, herbal and balanced, with honey, citrus, bitter orange, black tea and alpine herb notes.
More delicate and approachable than very dark amaros
bottles.edge: A modern, gentler amaro: moderate bitterness, floral and citrus-led rather than root-heavy.

bottles.name: Amaro Camatti
desc: Italian amaro from Genoa, herbal and fresh, with mint, aromatic herbs, soft spices and clean bitterness.
Fresher and more minty than darker amaros like Averna
bottles.edge: Bitter-root forward with a dry, savoury finish — closer to Fernet than to Averna, without the menthol blast.

bottles.name: Fragante Amaro Insolito
desc: Modern and aromatic Italian amaro, with herbal, citrusy, spiced notes and balanced bitterness.
Fresher and more fragrant than a classic dark amaro
bottles.edge: The outlier: aromatic and unconventional, built on fruit and flowers rather than the usual bitter roots.

bottles.name: Cynar
desc: Italian amaro made with artichoke, herbal, vegetal and sweet-bitter.
More earthy and less citrusy than many other amaros
bottles.origin: Italy — originally Padova; produced by Gruppo Campari, Milano
bottles.edge: Built on artichoke: vegetal and savoury-bitter rather than sweet-bitter, and low in alcohol. Excellent long with soda.

bottles.name: Fernet Branca
bottles.edge: The anchor for amari: the most bitter and most menthol bottle in the bar. Everything else on this shelf is softer than Fernet.

bottles.name: Branca Menta
bottles.fact: Formulated in Milan in 1845 by Bernardino Branca from 27 herbs, in a formula still kept secret.
bottles.edge: Fernet plus peppermint: the same bitter backbone with a sweet, cold mint front. Easier than Fernet, and served very cold.

bottles.name: Bordiga Fernet
bottles.fact: Herbalist Pietro Bordiga founded the distillery in Cuneo in 1888; it still uses wood-fired copper alembics.
bottles.edge: An alpine take on fernet: less menthol and more mountain herb than Branca, distilled on wood-fired copper.
bottles.tier: Premium for the botanicals and the still: Cuneo mountain herbs on wood-fired alembics, small batch.

bottles.name: Jefferson
bottles.fact: Made by Vecchio Magazzino Doganale near Cosenza, Calabria; its “Captain Jefferson” story is marketing legend, not history.
bottles.edge: A modern Italian amaro, balanced between citrus and bitter root — less sweet than Averna, less aggressive than Fernet.

bottles.name: Roger
bottles.fact: From Vecchio Magazzino Doganale, the tiny Calabrian house behind Jefferson and Frack — bottled at extra-strong proof.
bottles.edge: A gentle, citrus-driven digestivo — one of the lightest bitters on the shelf.

bottles.name: Dopolavoro
bottles.fact: Another small-batch amaro from Vecchio Magazzino Doganale, the Calabrian house behind Jefferson, Roger and Frack.
bottles.edge: “After work”: an easy-drinking amaro, moderately sweet, herbal and low in bitterness.

bottles.name: Frack
bottles.fact: Made in Montalto, Calabria at 24% ABV by Vecchio Magazzino Doganale, the house behind Jefferson and Roger.
bottles.edge: A dry, spice-led amaro with a bitter finish — closer to Camatti than to the sweet southern style.

bottles.name: Silvio Carta Estremista
bottles.fact: The Carta family's spirit-making tradition traces to 1939, infusing wild Sardinian botanicals into family-made spirit.
bottles.edge: Sardinian and deliberately extreme: one of the most intensely bitter bottles here after Fernet, with myrtle-country herbs.
bottles.tier: Premium for the small Sardinian production and the local botanicals — nothing industrial about it.

bottles.name: Liquore Strega
bottles.edge: Saffron-yellow and unmistakable: 70 herbs with saffron and mint, sweet rather than bitter. Its colour alone identifies it.

bottles.name: Liquirizia di Santa Maria
bottles.origin: Italy — Firenze (Tuscany), Officina Profumo-Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella
bottles.edge: Pure liquorice: black, sweet and salty-edged. Not an amaro — a single-flavour digestivo.

bottles.name: Abracadabra Liquirizia
bottles.fact: Made from Calabria's PDO Martorano licorice root, boiled and pressed by an ancestral method.
bottles.edge: A softer, sweeter liquorice than Santa Maria, with less salt and more sugar.

bottles.name: Rucolino Ischia
bottles.fact: Made by macerating wild arugula from Ischia's volcanic Monte Epomeo in high-proof alcohol, then resting a month.
bottles.edge: Made from rocket leaves on Ischia: green, peppery and vegetal — there is nothing else like it in the bar.
bottles.tier: Premium for the raw material: wild rocket grown on Ischia, a genuinely local and limited ingredient.

bottles.name: Alpe Genepy Herbet
bottles.fact: Founded in 1948 by Armando Calvetti in the Aosta Valley, hand-picking wild alpine genepy in strict amounts.
bottles.edge: Genepy: a single alpine wormwood species, so it is herbal-sweet and pine-fresh rather than bitter. The classic high-mountain digestivo.

bottles.name: Cappelletti Rabarbaro Sfumato
bottles.fact: Trento's Cappelletti herbalist shop, founded 1909, still makes this amaro from Chinese rhubarb grown wild in Trentino.
bottles.edge: Smoked rhubarb root — actually smoky on the nose, which no other bottle here is. Bitter, earthy, low in sugar.
bottles.tier: Premium for the ingredient treatment: Chinese rhubarb root smoked before infusion, an unusual and costly step.

bottles.name: Bordiga Elisir di China
bottles.fact: Herbalist Pietro Bordiga founded the distillery in Cuneo in 1888; it still uses wood-fired copper alembics.
bottles.edge: Cinchona bark elixir: quinine bitterness with cocoa, drier and more medicinal than an orange amaro.
bottles.tier: Premium for the herbalist recipe and wood-fired distillation.

bottles.name: Doragrossa Amaro di Torino
bottles.fact: Revives Turin's early-1900s apothecary shift from sweet liqueurs to bitter digestifs — rhubarb, gentian, juniper, fennel, cocoa.
bottles.edge: A Turin amaro in the classic city style: balanced bitter-sweet, more spice than citrus.

bottles.name: Anacardo Black
bottles.origin: Could not verify with confidence — flagged so this isn't presented as fact.
bottles.edge: Built on cashew fruit — nutty and dark, a flavour no other bottle on this shelf offers.

bottles.name: Rupes
bottles.fact: Cold-macerated 20 days from roughly 30 Calabrian herbs and roots; named for the Roccella cliff ("rupe").
bottles.edge: An alpine amaro with a distinctly rocky, mineral bitterness and low sugar.

bottles.name: Il Convento Limoncello
bottles.edge: The house limoncello: lemon zest and sugar, nothing bitter. Served frozen.

bottles.name: Citrange Limone
bottles.fact: Made from Sicilian citrus grown in volcanic soil near Etna, infused with native Sicilian wild herbs.
bottles.edge: A lemon liqueur with more bite than a classic limoncello — less sugar, more zest oil.

bottles.name: Citrange Mandarino
bottles.fact: Made from Sicilian citrus grown in volcanic soil near Etna, infused with native Sicilian wild herbs.
bottles.edge: The mandarin version: sweeter and rounder than the lemon, with tangerine peel aroma.

bottles.name: Mandarello
bottles.origin: Italy — Sicily (Etna area), Scialù / Spiriti Siciliani
bottles.edge: A mandarin liqueur, richer and more candied than Citrange Mandarino.

bottles.name: Il Convento Finocchietto
bottles.edge: Wild fennel liqueur: aniseed and green herb, sweet but savoury-edged. The digestivo to offer after a heavy plate.

bottles.name: Passito di Pantelleria
serves: Chilled, on its own as a dessert wine
Paired with pastry or blue cheese
bottles.edge: Not a liqueur but a sweet wine: sun-dried Zibibbo grapes from Pantelleria — apricot, honey and salt.
bottles.tier: Premium for the grape and the method: Zibibbo dried in the sun on the island, a labour-intensive passito with tiny yields. It is wine, so it is lighter and less sugary-thick than the liqueurs beside it.

bottles.name: Frangelico
bottles.edge: Hazelnut and vanilla, sweet and nutty — the dessert bottle, unmistakable by its friar-shaped bottle.

bottles.name: Amaretto Disaronno
bottles.edge: Almond-marzipan sweetness, no bitterness. Sweeter and rounder than Frangelico, with apricot-kernel aroma.

bottles.name: Luxardo Maraschino
bottles.edge: The benchmark maraschino: dry, funky and floral, distilled from whole Marasca cherries including the stones — which is why it tastes of almond, not of cherry syrup.
bottles.tier: Premium for the fruit and the method: Luxardo grows its own Marasca cherries and distils the whole fruit, then ages in ash wood for two years.

bottles.name: Stambecco Maraschino
bottles.edge: A rounder, sweeter maraschino than Luxardo — more cherry fruit, less dry almond funk.

bottles.name: Bordiga Maraschino
bottles.fact: Herbalist Pietro Bordiga founded the distillery in Cuneo in 1888; it still uses wood-fired copper alembics.
bottles.edge: The alpine maraschino: cleaner and more herbal than Luxardo, distilled on wood-fired copper.
bottles.tier: Premium for the small-batch wood-fired distillation.

bottles.name: Giocondo Caffè
bottles.fact: This Calabrian coffee liqueur blends Ethiopian coffee with home-roasted acorns, plus vanilla, bitter orange and cinchona.
bottles.edge: A coffee liqueur on the sweeter, more chocolatey side.

bottles.name: Borghetti Coffee Liqueur
bottles.edge: Real espresso, low sugar: the drier and more bitter of the two coffee bottles, and the one for an Espresso Martini.

bottles.name: Cappelletti Mirtillo
bottles.edge: Blueberry: fresh fruit rather than syrup, tart-sweet, and the only berry liqueur on the shelf.

bottles.name: Appleton Estate
desc: Jamaican rum with good body, showing ripe banana, caramel, vanilla, spice, and oak notes.
It has more character than a white or neutral rum
bottles.edge: Jamaican pot still: funky, with the estate’s signature orange peel and molasses. The rum with the most character in a Daiquiri.

bottles.name: Flor de Caña 12yrs
desc: Aged Nicaraguan rum, smooth and dry, with caramel, vanilla, dried fruit, soft spice, and oak notes.
Less sweet than many commercial rums
bottles.edge: Nicaraguan, twelve years in bourbon barrels at volcanic altitude, with no added sugar — drier than Diplomatico and cleaner than Appleton.
bottles.tier: Premium for the age and the honesty: 12 years slow-aged, zero sugar added, which is rare in this category. It tastes drier than rums with the same age precisely because nothing was added back.

bottles.name: Diplomatico Reserva
desc: Smooth, rounded and slightly sweeter Venezuelan rum, with caramel, vanilla, chocolate, dried fruit and soft spice notes.
Richer and easier to sip than a dry rum
bottles.edge: Venezuelan and openly sweet: heavy, chocolatey and dessert-like. The rum for a guest who wants sweetness, not funk.

bottles.name: Espolón Blanco
desc: Mexican tequila with a fresh, easy-drinking and very versatile profile.
It has agave, citrus and soft pepper notes
bottles.fact: Espolón's skeleton-art labels are hand-etched into scratchboard by illustrator Steven Noble, evoking Mexican folk art.
bottles.edge: The anchor for agave: 100% blue agave, peppery and clean, made for cocktails. Everything else here is compared to this.

bottles.name: Espolón Reposado
desc: Mexican reposado tequila, smoother and rounder than Espolón Blanco.
It keeps agave and citrus notes, but adds vanilla, soft spice and a touch of oak
bottles.edge: Blanco rested a few months in oak: softer, with vanilla and caramel over the agave pepper.

bottles.name: Espolón Añejo
desc: Mexican añejo tequila aged in oak, smoother, deeper and fuller than the Reposado.
It has cooked agave, vanilla, caramel, spice and soft oak notes
bottles.fact: Espolón's skeleton-art labels are hand-etched into scratchboard by illustrator Steven Noble, evoking Mexican folk art.
bottles.edge: A year in oak: darker, sweeter and closer to a whiskey. Sip it rather than shake it.

bottles.name: Herradura Plata
desc: Mexican blanco tequila, fresh and clean, with agave, citrus, and soft pepper notes.
A bit more serious and premium than a basic blanco tequila
bottles.edge: Rested 45 days, unusual for a blanco, so it is rounder and less sharp than Espolón Blanco while staying agave-forward.
bottles.tier: Premium for the estate: 100% agave, estate-grown, with natural yeast fermentation and a longer rest than a standard silver.

bottles.name: Fortaleza Blanco
desc: Mexican blanco tequila with a more artisanal style, fresh and full of agave flavor.
It has cooked agave, citrus, soft pepper, and a light mineral touch
bottles.fact: Fortaleza crushes agave with an antique stone tahona wheel, distilled in three small handmade copper pot stills.
bottles.edge: The traditional one: agave cooked in a stone oven, crushed by a tahona stone wheel, fermented with wild yeast. Much sweeter, oilier and more vegetal than Espolón.
bottles.tier: Premium for the method: brick oven, tahona stone crushing and copper pot stills — a slow, low-yield process almost nobody still uses. That is exactly what you taste as cooked-agave sweetness.

bottles.name: Fortaleza Reposado
desc: Mexican reposado tequila with an artisanal style, smooth and full of agave flavor.
It keeps the freshness of the blanco, but adds vanilla, soft caramel, spice, and delicate oak
bottles.edge: The tahona blanco with light oak: the agave still leads, now with butterscotch. Far more agave-forward than Espolón Reposado.
bottles.tier: Premium for the same tahona process, then a short rest in American oak.

bottles.name: Fortaleza Añejo
desc: Mexican añejo tequila with an artisanal style, smooth, deep and full of cooked agave flavour.
It has vanilla, caramel, spice, soft oak and a light mineral touch
bottles.edge: Eighteen months in oak but the agave still shows — where most añejos taste of wood, this one still tastes of the plant.
bottles.tier: Premium for the tahona process carried through a long ageing without losing the agave character.

bottles.name: Illegal Joven
desc: Young mezcal, fresh and smoky, with agave, herbs, soft citrus, and a mineral touch.
More direct and expressive than a reposado.
bottles.edge: Espadín agave roasted in an underground pit: smoke plus green fruit. Smoke is the whole difference between mezcal and tequila — start a guest here.

bottles.name: Illegal Reposado
desc: Reposado mezcal, smoky and rounder than the Joven, with agave, soft vanilla, spice, and light oak notes.
It keeps the mezcal character but feels smoother
bottles.fact: Founder John Rexer began by carrying mezcal from Oaxaca into Guatemala by bus, in duffel bags.
bottles.edge: Four months in American oak: the smoke softens and vanilla comes in. The bridge between mezcal and whiskey.

bottles.name: Illegal Añejo
desc: Añejo mezcal, smoother, deeper and more elegant than the Reposado, with delicate smoke, cooked agave, vanilla, caramel, spice and oak notes.
Fuller and more complex
bottles.edge: Thirteen months in oak: the most whisky-like agave spirit here, smoke folded into caramel and spice.
bottles.tier: Premium for the ageing: over a year in oak on an artisanal, small-batch mezcal.

bottles.name: Don Amado Reposado
desc: Artisanal reposado mezcal, smoky but elegant, with cooked agave, soft vanilla, spice, and delicate oak notes.
Fuller than a joven mezcal, but still keeps that mineral and smoky character
bottles.fact: Made by Oaxaca's Arellanes family at Real de Mina, distilled in traditional clay pot stills, not copper.
bottles.edge: Distilled in clay pots rather than copper, an old Oaxacan technique — earthier and more mineral than Illegal, with softer smoke.
bottles.tier: Premium for the method: clay-pot distillation, an ancestral technique with tiny yields, which is what gives it the earthen, mineral note.

bottles.name: Vodka Altamura
desc: Premium Italian vodka, clean and smooth, made from Altamura wheat.
It has a rounder texture than a basic vodka
bottles.edge: Made from durum wheat grown in Puglia — a slightly bready, rounded vodka rather than a neutral one.
bottles.tier: Premium for the grain: Altamura durum wheat, the same wheat as the region’s DOP bread, distilled locally.

bottles.name: Vodka Vulcanica
desc: Clean and smooth Italian vodka, with a neutral profile but good presence.
Easy to mix and doesn't overpower other flavours
bottles.edge: Filtered through volcanic rock from Sicily: a mineral, slightly saline finish that neutral vodkas do not have.
bottles.tier: Premium for the source: Etna spring water and volcanic filtration.

bottles.name: Grey Goose
desc: Premium French vodka, very clean, smooth and elegant.
It has a round and silky texture
bottles.edge: French winter wheat and Cognac-region spring water: soft, sweet and creamy — the roundest vodka on the shelf.
bottles.tier: Premium for the ingredients and the water: Picardie winter wheat distilled once, with limestone-filtered water from Gensac. The softness is what people pay for.

bottles.name: Belvedere
desc: Premium Polish vodka, clean and smooth, made from rye.
It has a slightly creamier profile with a bit more character than a very neutral vodka
bottles.edge: Polish rye, not wheat: drier and more peppery than Grey Goose, with a spicy finish. The one for a Martini rather than for sipping.
bottles.tier: Premium for the grain and the rules: 100% Dankowskie rye and Polska Wódka appellation, no additives at all.

bottles.name: Tanqueray
desc: Classic London Dry gin, dry, clean and juniper-forward.
It has citrus, soft spice and herbal notes
bottles.origin: United Kingdom — distilled at Cameronbridge, Scotland (London Dry style)
bottles.edge: The anchor for gin: four botanicals, juniper first, nothing decorative. Every other gin here is described as more floral, more citric or softer than this.

bottles.name: Tanqueray No.10
desc: Premium Tanqueray gin, fresher and more citrus-forward than the classic, with grapefruit, lime, orange, and juniper notes.
More elegant and bright
bottles.origin: United Kingdom — distilled at Cameronbridge, Scotland
bottles.edge: Tanqueray built on fresh whole citrus rather than dried peel — grapefruit and lime on the nose, much rounder than the standard.
bottles.tier: Premium for the raw material: whole fresh grapefruit, orange and lime distilled in a small still (“Tiny Ten”). Fresh fruit costs far more than dried peel and gives the aroma its brightness.

bottles.name: Monkey 47 dry
desc: Premium German gin, very aromatic and complex, with juniper, citrus, herbs, spices, and a floral touch.
It has more layers than a classic London Dry
bottles.fact: Contains exactly 47 botanicals, distilled in Germany's Black Forest by founder Alexander Stein.
bottles.edge: 47 botanicals at 47% — the most complex gin on the shelf. Cranberry from the Black Forest gives it a tart, spicy edge no London Dry has.
bottles.tier: Premium for the botanical count and the rest: 47 botanicals, a third of them from the Black Forest, macerated then rested three months in earthenware. That rest is why it is intense but not harsh.

bottles.name: Monkey 47 Sloe
desc: German gin infused with sloe berries, with red fruit, plum, soft spice, and a herbal touch.
Sweeter, fruitier, and rounder than a dry gin
bottles.edge: The sweet, deep-red version: sloe berries steeped in the dry gin. Fruit-driven, lower proof, drink it neat or in a Negroni variation.
bottles.tier: Premium for the fruit: hand-picked wild sloes on top of an already premium gin base.

bottles.name: Hendrick's
desc: Smooth and aromatic Scottish gin, with cucumber, rose, citrus, and juniper notes.
More floral and delicate than a classic London Dry
bottles.edge: Cucumber and rose infused after distillation — the least juniper-forward gin here, and the reason it is served with cucumber rather than lime.

bottles.name: Four Pillars Rare Dry
desc: Australian dry gin, aromatic and citrusy, with juniper, orange, spice and herbal notes.
It has more character and aroma than a simple London Dry
bottles.edge: Australian: whole oranges in the still plus native pepperberry, so it is citrus-sweet up front with a peppery finish Tanqueray does not have.
bottles.tier: Premium for the ingredients and scale: whole fresh Australian oranges and native Tasmanian pepperberry, distilled in small batches on a German copper still.

bottles.name: Four Pillars Bloody Shiraz
desc: Australian gin infused with Shiraz grapes, with red fruit, plum, soft spice, and juniper notes.
Fruitier and slightly sweeter than a dry gin
bottles.edge: Shiraz grapes steeped in gin for eight weeks — deep purple, jammy and tannic. Closer to a fruit liqueur than a gin.
bottles.tier: Premium for the grape: Yarra Valley Shiraz, whole bunches steeped and pressed. The tannin from the grape skins is what stops it tasting like syrup.

bottles.name: Four Pillars Navy Strength
desc: Stronger and bolder Australian gin, with higher alcohol, more body and bigger flavour.
It has juniper, citrus, spice and herbal notes
bottles.edge: 58.8% — the strongest gin here. Ginger and turmeric give it heat; it holds its shape in a drink where a 40% gin gets lost.

bottles.name: Four Pillars Olive Leaf
desc: Australian gin with a more Mediterranean, herbal and savoury profile, made with olive leaf.
It has olive, rosemary, lemon, juniper and a light savoury touch
bottles.edge: Savoury rather than sweet: olive leaf, olives and rosemary make it briny. The gin for a Dirty Martini.
bottles.tier: Premium for the ingredients: Australian olive leaf and green olives, a genuinely unusual botanical bill.

bottles.name: Four Pillars Yuzu
desc: Fresh and citrusy Australian gin, with yuzu, lemon, mandarin, juniper, and a light herbal touch.
Brighter and more exotic than a classic citrus gin
bottles.edge: Fresh yuzu, sharper and more perfumed than any lemon gin here. Bright, short and very citric.
bottles.tier: Premium for the fruit: fresh yuzu, an expensive and short-season citrus.

bottles.name: Roku
desc: Smooth, clean and aromatic Japanese gin, with yuzu, green tea, cherry blossom, sansho pepper and juniper notes.
More delicate and floral than a classic London Dry
bottles.edge: Japanese, six Japanese botanicals including sakura flower and yuzu, each harvested in its own season. Softer and more delicate than Tanqueray.
bottles.tier: Premium for the sourcing: six Japanese botanicals picked at their individual peak seasons and distilled separately by Suntory.

bottles.name: Gin Mare
desc: Spanish Mediterranean-style gin, herbal and aromatic, with olive, rosemary, thyme, basil, citrus and juniper notes.
More savoury and food-friendly than a classic gin
bottles.edge: Mediterranean and savoury: olive, rosemary, thyme and basil. The clearest alternative to a juniper gin — pour it when a guest wants a G&T that tastes of herbs.
bottles.tier: Premium for the method: each botanical macerated and distilled separately, with Arbequina olives from Spain.

bottles.name: Gin Mare Capri
desc: Spanish Mediterranean-style gin, more citrusy and fresh than classic Gin Mare, with lemon, bergamot, Mediterranean herbs, olive and juniper notes.
Brighter and more summery
bottles.edge: Gin Mare with Capri lemon added — brighter and more citric than the standard, same savoury base.
bottles.tier: Premium and limited: Capri lemons on the small-batch Gin Mare process.

bottles.name: Occitan Gin
desc: Italian gin by Bordiga, dry, clean and herbal with strong alpine juniper character.
It has citrus, cardamom and mountain herb notes
bottles.edge: Southern French: lavender and Provençal herbs, floral where Gin Mare is savoury.
bottles.tier: Premium for the regional botanicals and small production.

bottles.name: Glendalough Rose
desc: Smooth and floral Irish gin, infused with wild rose and fresh rose petals.
It has rose petal, soft red fruit, citrus and juniper notes
bottles.edge: Irish, distilled with fresh wild rose petals — the most floral and perfumed gin here.
bottles.tier: Premium for the botanicals: foraged Irish botanicals picked fresh and distilled the same day.

bottles.name: Boigin Sardinia
desc: Italian gin from Sardinia, fresh and Mediterranean, with juniper, citrus, aromatic herbs and a light salty touch.
More herbal and coastal than a classic London Dry
bottles.edge: Sardinian: myrtle and island herbs give it a resinous, Mediterranean scrub character.
bottles.tier: Premium for the local wild botanicals and small-island production.

bottles.name: Portofino
desc: Premium Italian gin, fresh and aromatic, inspired by the Portofino coast.
It has juniper, lemon, Mediterranean herbs and floral notes
bottles.edge: Ligurian: fresh basil, lavender and citrus from the coast — lighter and more perfumed than Gin Mare.
bottles.tier: Premium for the fresh Ligurian botanicals, some picked in the surrounding hills.

bottles.name: Malfy Rosa Grapefruit
desc: Fresh and fruity Italian gin, with clear pink grapefruit, citrus, and a touch of juniper.
Sweeter and easier to drink than a classic London Dry
bottles.origin: Italy — Moncalieri, Torino (Piedmont), with citrus from the Amalfi Coast
bottles.edge: Sicilian pink grapefruit, sweet and easy — the least juniper of the Malfy line and a Spritz-friendly gin.

bottles.name: Malfy Limone
desc: Fresh and citrusy Italian gin, with clear lemon, citrus peel, and soft juniper notes.
Brighter and more refreshing than a classic London Dry
bottles.origin: Italy — Moncalieri, Torino (Piedmont), with citrus from the Amalfi Coast
bottles.edge: Amalfi lemon peel, sharp and simple. The straightforward citrus gin for a G&T with a lemon wheel.

bottles.name: Aviation
desc: Smooth and balanced American gin, with less juniper than a classic London Dry.
It has citrus, floral notes, soft spice, and a herbal touch
bottles.edge: American: lavender and sarsaparilla, low juniper, soft and rounded. Built for cocktails rather than a G&T.

bottles.name: Tenjaku Gin
desc: Smooth, clean and easy-drinking Japanese gin, with juniper, citrus, herbs and a light floral touch.
More delicate than a classic London Dry
bottles.edge: Japanese and delicate: yuzu and green tea over soft Mount Fuji water. Lighter than Roku, very smooth.

bottles.name: Cil The Authentic Rural
desc: Artisanal Italian gin, fresh and Mediterranean, with juniper, lemon, citrus, aromatic herbs, and a mineral touch.
It has more personality than a classic London Dry
bottles.edge: Sardinian rural botanicals, dry and earthy — herb-led rather than citrus-led.
bottles.tier: Premium for the small-batch Sardinian production.

bottles.name: Cil The Authentic Torbato
desc: Italian gin from Calabria, more intense and unique, with a citrusy, herbal and lightly smoky profile.
It has juniper, lemon, Mediterranean herbs and a touch of peat
bottles.edge: The unusual one: built with Torbato, a rare Sardinian white grape, which gives it a vinous, wine-like body no other gin here has.
bottles.tier: Premium for the grape: Torbato is a rare Sardinian variety grown almost nowhere else, and its wine base is what makes this gin taste of grape and salt.

bottles.name: Glen Grant Arboralis
desc: Smooth and fruity single malt scotch, with apple, pear, honey, vanilla, and light oak notes.
Fresh and easy to drink
bottles.fact: Glen Grant's squat, helmet-shaped stills use copper purifiers that reflux heavy vapors for a light, fresh character.
bottles.edge: Speyside, no age statement: light, apple-and-honey, the gentlest whisky on the shelf. A good first single malt.

bottles.name: Glen Grant 10yrs
desc: Smooth, fresh and fruity single malt scotch, with green apple, pear, honey, vanilla and light oak notes.
Cleaner and more elegant than Arboralis
bottles.edge: The same orchard-fruit style with ten years of oak: more vanilla and length than Arboralis, still no smoke.
bottles.tier: Premium for the age statement: ten years in cask, which buys depth and a longer finish over the no-age Arboralis.

bottles.name: Glen Grant 15yrs
desc: Single malt scotch, more elegant and fuller than Glen Grant 10, with ripe fruit, honey, vanilla, soft spice, and oak notes.
Still fresh and fruity, but with more depth
bottles.fact: Glen Grant's squat, helmet-shaped stills use copper purifiers that reflux heavy vapors for a light, fresh character.
bottles.edge: Fifteen years in first-fill American oak: much richer than the 10 — toffee, spice and real weight.
bottles.tier: Premium for the ageing: 15 years, largely first-fill oak. Next to the 10 it is darker, sweeter and considerably longer, and the price is the extra five years of evaporation.

bottles.name: Laphroaig 10yrs
desc: Islay single malt scotch, intense and smoky, with peat, sea salt, oak, spice, and a light medicinal touch.
Much stronger and smokier than Glen Grant
bottles.edge: The medicinal one: Islay peat with iodine and seaweed. Even next to Ardbeg it reads more antiseptic than sooty. Guests either love it or should be steered away.

bottles.name: Monkey Shoulder
desc: Smooth, rounded blended malt scotch, with vanilla, honey, soft fruit and light spice notes.
Less intense than a smoky single malt
bottles.edge: A blended malt built for mixing: sweet, soft, no smoke. The whisky to use in a cocktail, not to sip.

bottles.name: Ardbeg 10yrs
desc: Islay single malt scotch, intense, smoky and full of character.
It has peat, smoke, sea salt, citrus and spice notes
bottles.edge: Islay peat too, but sooty and citric rather than medicinal — smoke with a sweet, lemony core where Laphroaig goes iodine.

bottles.name: Glenmorangie 12yrs
desc: Smooth, elegant and fruity single malt scotch, with orange, honey, vanilla, ripe fruit and delicate oak notes.
Much easier and gentler than a smoky Islay
bottles.edge: Distilled in Scotland’s tallest stills, which is why it is so light and floral — peach and vanilla, zero smoke.
bottles.tier: Premium for the cask and the still: extra-tall copper stills for a lighter spirit, then finishing casks. The refinement is in the delicacy, not in power.

bottles.name: Macallan 12yrs Double Cask
desc: Elegant and smooth single malt scotch, matured in American and European sherry-seasoned oak casks.
It has honey, vanilla, dried fruit, caramel, soft spice, and oak notes
bottles.edge: Sherry-driven: dried fruit, orange and Christmas spice. The sweetest and most sherried whisky here.
bottles.tier: Premium for the wood: matured in both American and European sherry-seasoned oak, which Macallan seasons itself in Jerez. Sherry casks cost many times an ex-bourbon barrel — that is where the dried-fruit richness comes from.

bottles.name: Sexton Single Malt
desc: Irish single malt whiskey, smooth and easy to drink, with honey, dried fruit, soft chocolate, and light oak notes.
More delicate and rounded than many stronger whiskies
bottles.edge: Irish single malt aged entirely in Spanish oloroso sherry casks — dark and fruity where most Irish whiskey is light.

bottles.name: Redbreast 12yrs
desc: Premium Irish whiskey, smooth but full-bodied, with honey, dried fruit, spice, vanilla, and oak notes.
More complex and elegant than a basic Irish whiskey
bottles.edge: Single pot still: made from both malted and unmalted barley, an Irish-only style that gives it a thick, creamy, spicy texture no single malt has.
bottles.tier: Premium for the style and the casks: traditional single pot still production, triple distilled, matured in bourbon and oloroso sherry casks. That unmalted barley is why it coats the mouth.

bottles.name: Wild Turkey 81
desc: Smooth and easy-drinking American bourbon, with vanilla, caramel, sweet corn, and soft oak notes.
Lighter than Wild Turkey 101
bottles.fact: Wild Turkey barrels its bourbon at 115 proof, below the legal max of 125, to preserve flavor.
bottles.edge: The entry bourbon: 40.5%, sweet corn and vanilla, easy in a highball.

bottles.name: Wild Turkey 101
desc: American bourbon, stronger and bolder than Wild Turkey 81, with vanilla, caramel, spice, and oak notes.
Fuller and more present
bottles.fact: Wild Turkey barrels its bourbon at 115 proof, below the legal max of 125, to preserve flavor.
bottles.edge: The same bourbon at 50.5% — much more spice, oak and heat. This is the one that survives ice and citrus in a sour.

bottles.name: Wild Turkey Rye
desc: American rye whiskey, drier and spicier than bourbon.
It has pepper, vanilla, soft caramel and oak notes
bottles.edge: Rye instead of corn-heavy mash: drier, peppery and spicy, less sweet than either bourbon. The right base for a Manhattan.

bottles.name: Wild Turkey Longbranch
desc: Smooth and refined American bourbon, with vanilla, caramel, soft oak, and a delicate smoky touch.
More elegant and easier to sip than Wild Turkey 101
bottles.fact: Created with Matthew McConaughey, Longbranch is twice-filtered through oak, then Texas mesquite charcoal, for subtle smokiness.
bottles.edge: Filtered through Texas mesquite and oak charcoal — a light smokiness the other Turkeys do not have.
bottles.tier: Premium for the finishing: refined with Jimmy Russell and Matthew McConaughey, filtered through mesquite charcoal, in small batches.

bottles.name: Rittenhouse Rye
desc: Bold American rye whiskey, dry and spicy, with pepper, vanilla, caramel, and oak notes.
Stronger and more characterful than a soft rye
bottles.edge: Bottled-in-bond at 50%: a legally defined standard — one distillery, one season, at least four years, 100 proof. Dry, spicy and the bartender’s rye.

bottles.name: Michters Small Batch Bourbon
desc: Smooth and elegant American bourbon, with vanilla, caramel, ripe fruit, soft spice, and oak notes.
Rounder and more refined than a basic bourbon
bottles.edge: Soft and caramel-sweet, low proof and very approachable — the least spicy American on the shelf.
bottles.tier: Premium for the process: small batches, barrel entry at low proof and heat-cycled warehouses, all of which cost yield in exchange for softness.

bottles.name: Woodford Reserve
desc: Elegant and balanced American bourbon, with vanilla, caramel, dried fruit, soft spice, and oak notes.
It has good body without being aggressive
bottles.edge: Balanced and clean: part pot-still distilled, dried fruit and vanilla, less aggressive than Wild Turkey 101.
bottles.tier: Premium for the distillation: copper pot stills alongside column distillate, unusual for bourbon and the reason it is rounder.

bottles.name: Woodford Reserve Double Oak
desc: American bourbon, richer and deeper than classic Woodford Reserve, with more oak influence.
It has vanilla, caramel, chocolate, toasted oak, and soft spice notes
bottles.edge: The standard Woodford put into a second, deeply toasted new barrel — much sweeter, with caramel and chocolate. Double the oak, double the sweetness.
bottles.tier: Premium for the second maturation: a full extra new charred oak barrel per batch, deeply toasted and lightly charred.

bottles.name: Tenjaku Pure Malt
desc: Smooth and balanced Japanese whisky, with ripe fruit, honey, cereal, and delicate oak notes.
Clean and easy to drink
bottles.edge: Japanese blended malt: soft, floral and lightly honeyed, the gentlest whisky in the bar after Arboralis.

bottles.name: Nikka From The Barrel
desc: Intense Japanese whisky with more body and strength than many softer Japanese whiskies.
It has caramel, spice, ripe fruit and oak notes
bottles.origin: Japan — blend of Nikka's Yoichi and Miyagikyo distilleries
bottles.edge: 51.4% and undiluted-style: the most concentrated whisky here. Blended from Yoichi and Miyagikyo, then married in barrels before bottling.
bottles.tier: Premium for the blend and the strength: Nikka marries the blended whisky in casks for a further period and bottles at high strength, so nothing is watered down. Enormous flavour for its size.

bottles.name: Vecchia Romagna
desc: Smooth and aromatic Italian brandy, with dried fruit, vanilla, spice, and oak notes.
Warm and rounded
bottles.edge: Italian brandy from Trebbiano grapes: sweeter and softer than a Cognac, with vanilla and dried fruit from oak ageing.
